2.75 2.76 2.77 The wise man should always avoid these three: a wicked king, a wicked friend, and a wicked wife; for they cause the destruction of one's own self.
Just as a fire, when fanned by the wind, consumes even a forest, so too does a kingdom, when led by a wicked king, perish along with its subjects.
One should not dwell in a place where there is no king, nor in a place where the king is weak, nor in a place where the king is cruel, nor in a place where the king is a slave to his senses.

3.75 3.76 3.77 The wise man should not be distressed by the loss of wealth, nor should he rejoice at its acquisition; for both gain and loss are subject to change. When one’s wealth is lost, one should not grieve, nor should one exult when it is gained; for both prosperity and adversity are transient.
One should not be elated by success, nor dejected by failure; for fortune is fickle and moves like the wind.

5.20 5.21 5.22 The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this is the first great miracle of the Tathāgata, which has not been seen by previous Tathāgatas, nor will it be seen by future Tathāgatas, and is not seen even by present Tathāgatas. What is that miracle? It is this: when the Tathāgata wishes, he can emit from his body a stream of fire, and from his mouth a stream of water; and conversely, he can emit from his mouth a stream of fire, and from his body a stream of water. This, Ānanda, is the first great miracle of the Tathāgata. Then the Blessed One, having performed this great miracle, rose from his seat and entered the village of Piṇḍola for alms. Having walked for alms in Piṇḍola, after the meal, on his return from alms-round, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the village of Piṇḍola and inform the householder Citta: ‘Householder, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered the village of Piṇḍola for alms. When you have finished your meal, you may come to see the Blessed One. “As you command, Lord,” replied the Venerable Ānanda, and having done so, he returned to the Blessed One and reported: “Lord, I have informed the householder Citta as you instructed. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered the village of Piṇḍola for alms. After walking for alms in Piṇḍola, after the meal, on his return from alms-round, he went to the residence of the householder Citta. At that time, the householder Citta was seated with a large assembly of Licchavis, discussing various worldly matters. Seeing the Blessed One approaching from afar, the householder Citta rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and paid homage with his head at the feet of the Blessed One. He then sat down to one side. As the householder Citta sat there, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma. Then the householder Citta, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dharma, addressed the Blessed One: “Lord, please enter the inner chamber; let the Blessed One rest for a while. “Enough, householder, I have finished my meal for today. Then the householder Citta, taking a low seat, sat down to one side. As he sat there, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma. Then the householder Citta, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dharma, said to the Blessed One: “Lord, let the Blessed One accept tomorrow’s meal from me, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Then the householder Citta, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then the householder Citta, having had excellent food—both hard and soft—prepared in his own residence, had the time announced to the Blessed One: “It is time, Lord; the meal is ready. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered the residence of the householder Citta with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. At that time, the householder Citta was preparing a pavilion in his residence, thinking: “I shall provide a place for the Blessed One to teach the Dharma to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then the Blessed One, having entered the residence of the householder Citta, sat down on the prepared seat in the pavilion with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. The householder Citta, having served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with his own hands with excellent food—both hard and soft—and having satisfied them, withdrew to one side. As the householder Citta sat there to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma. Then the householder Citta, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dharma, addressed the Blessed One: “Lord, let the Blessed One accept a dwelling from me; let the Blessed One reside in it. “Enough, householder, the Tathāgatas do not accept dwellings. A second and a third time the householder Citta made the same request, and the Blessed One gave the same reply. Then the householder Citta thought: “The Blessed One does not accept a dwelling from me; what if I were to build a dwelling for the Blessed One? Then the householder Citta went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he sat there, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma. Then the householder Citta, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dharma, addressed the Blessed One: “Lord, let the Blessed One accept a dwelling from me; let the Blessed One reside in it. “Householder, if you wish to build a dwelling for the Tathāgata, build it at Sāvatthī; there the Tathāgata will reside. “As you command, Lord,” replied the householder Citta, and rising from his seat, he paid homage to the Blessed One and, keeping him on his right, departed. Then the householder Citta, having returned to his residence, assembled the guildsmen and announced: “Gentlemen, the Blessed One has commanded me: ‘If you wish to build a dwelling for the Tathāgata, build it at Sāvatthī; there the Tathāgata will reside. Therefore, gentlemen, let us build a dwelling for the Blessed One at Sāvatthī. “Very well, householder,” they replied. 5.116. When the king has been slain, his son, who is capable of protecting the earth, should be consecrated; for it is better that one man should rule than that the kingdom should fall into disorder. If there is no son, a kinsman belonging to the same lineage (sagotra) or even a minister should be made king by those who desire the welfare of the people. One should not allow the royal power to pass to a person of low character, nor to one who is greedy, nor to one who is cruel, nor to one who is addicted to vice. For when the kingdom is governed by such a person, the subjects quickly perish like cattle without a herdsman. Therefore, having examined the qualities of the candidates, one should install a virtuous man who is capable of upholding both the law and the state. Thus, the kingdom remains stable and free from internal strife, and the people live in peace under the protection of a righteous ruler.
